title: Time zones
summary: Naive and aware timestamps, converting from UTC, and why a 'day' depends on where you are.

steps.title: Naive and aware
body: `pd.Timestamp("2024-07-01 12:00")` is **naive**: it doesn't say *where* it is 12:00. Servers usually log in **UTC**.
utc = t.tz_localize("UTC")                 # attach a zone: same clock time, now known to be UTC
`tz_localize` says what zone a naive time was already in; `tz_convert` moves an aware time to another clock.
The rule of thumb: **store and compute in UTC, convert to local only to report.**

steps.prompt: A log line says `2024-07-01 12:00` and you know the server writes UTC. You want it on a New York clock. Which is right?
steps.explain: First say what the naive time *is* (UTC), then convert. Localizing straight to New York would claim it was noon in New York, which is a different instant; `tz_convert` on a naive time raises an error.
Tokyo is UTC+9. New York is UTC-4 in July (daylight saving), so noon UTC is 8 in the morning there.

steps.title: A day is local
body: "Sales per day" depends on whose day. An order at `2024-05-01 23:30` UTC was placed on **2 May** in Tokyo and on
**1 May** in New York. So convert first, then group:
ts = pd.to_datetime(df["ts"], utc=True)            # text ending in Z or +00:00 becomes UTC-aware
Daylight saving makes local days 23 or 25 hours long, so never assume a local day has 24 hourly rows.
For an aware index, call `df.index.tz_convert(...)` or `df.tz_convert(...)` directly.

steps.prompt: Match each call to what it does.
pairs: labels a naive time as UTC, clock unchanged
shows the same instant on a Paris clock
drops the zone, keeping the clock time
parses text straight into UTC-aware times
converts a whole column of aware times

steps.explain: A trailing `Z` (or `+00:00`) in the text is a zone, so pandas parses it as UTC-aware.

steps.title: Local hours
prompt: Write `local_hours(df, zone)`. `df` has a `ts` column of UTC timestamps as text, like `"2024-05-01T13:05:00Z"`.
Return the list of hours (ints 0 to 23) of those moments on the `zone` clock.
hints: The hours come out on the UTC clock. Parse with `utc=True` and convert.

steps.prompt: Daylight saving started in New York on 10 March 2024. What does this print?
steps.explain: Clocks jumped from 2:00 to 3:00 on 10 March, so that local day lasted only 23 hours.

steps.title: Daily counts in the right zone
prompt: Write `daily_local(df, zone)`. `df` has a `ts` column of UTC text timestamps (ending in `Z`), one row per event.
Return a dict from **local** date (`"2024-05-01"`) to the number of events on that date on the `zone` clock.
# 2024-05-01T23:30:00Z is 2 May in Tokyo but 1 May in New York
solution: return {day: int(n) for day, n in counts.items()}
hints: Format each local time as its date text with `.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")`, then count with `value_counts()`.
Turn the counts into a dict of plain ints.
